Continue to carefully observe the ECG.
questions.explanation: Go to the head of the bed to assist the anesthesia provider. The review tests active preparation and coordinated assistance for a potential cardiac event; simply watching the ECG is insufficient. Treatment and further escalation depend on rhythm, perfusion, and stability.
optionExplanations: Preparing these drugs without a provider-directed plan is not the appropriate initial response to the tachycardia.
Provides immediate, active assistance to assess and manage the developing cardiac problem.
Emergency equipment may be needed, but the key prioritizes immediate assistance to the anesthesia provider.
Passive observation alone does not provide the assistance and preparation the situation requires.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

additionalReferences.name: AHA · Tachyarrhythmia with a pulse algorithm (2025)

questions.currentGuidance: The stem does not provide blood pressure, perfusion, or the exact tachyarrhythmia. Immediate assistance is the intended nursing priority, while urgency, equipment, and treatment depend on assessment of stability and rhythm. Do not infer a particular drug treatment from the heart rate alone.

questions.prompt: James, 16 years old, has been admitted for an elbow injury after a skateboarding accident. When the perioperative nurse is prepping the elbow for a closed reduction and percutaneous pinning, what sequence should be used to perform the skin prep?
options: From tips of fingers, up the hand, wrist and forearm to above the elbow
From shoulder, axilla, upper arm, to below the elbow
From the elbow to the wrist and hand, and from the elbow to the shoulder including axilla
From the shoulder, down the upper arm to the elbow, including axilla and chest wall
questions.explanation: Prepare from the planned elbow operative site toward the periphery with fresh applicators and site-appropriate technique. Address the hand and axilla as higher-contamination areas without bringing used applicators back to the incision.
optionExplanations: Starts away from the intended incision and can carry contaminants toward it.
Starts at the axilla rather than the elbow operative site.
Starts at the incision region and works outward.
Does not describe preparing the distal operative surroundings from the elbow outward.

origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: What equipment would the circulating nurse activate last when preparing for a laparoscopy?
options: Video camera
Light source
Insufflator
Electrosurgical unit
questions.explanation: Keep the light source off or on standby until the fiber-optic connections are secure and the tip is controlled. Activating an exposed light cable can cause thermal injury or ignite drapes.
optionExplanations: Camera setup does not create the exposed hot-light-cable hazard.
The light source is activated after safe connection and positioning.
Has different tubing and flow checks, but does not explain the hot-cable sequence.
Uses its own safe standby procedures; the question specifically tests light-cable heat risk.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Waters, 33 years old, is scheduled for a laparoscopic tubal ligation. She weighs 124 kg. A hydrophobic filter is attached to the insufflator, which is placed above the operative level. In creating pneumoperitoneum, the insufflation pressure is set at 20 mmHg and the patient is placed in Trendelenburg. What patient complications should the circulating nurse anticipate?
options: Back flow of body fluid or gas into the insufflator
Increased cardiac output and hemodynamic instability
Subcutaneous emphysema and respiratory impairment
Vaginal bleeding and abdominal irritability
questions.explanation: High pneumoperitoneum pressure and Trendelenburg can impair ventilation, especially with obesity, and gas may dissect into tissues. Monitor respiratory and hemodynamic effects and use the provider's individualized pressure target.
optionExplanations: The filter and higher insufflator placement address backflow; this is not the principal patient complication asked.
Cardiac output may be reduced rather than predictably increased.
Matches the respiratory and gas-dissection risks.
Does not describe the major physiological effects of pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning.

questions.prompt: The circulating nurse has opened instrumentation to repair a fractured pelvis. She receives word that the patient needs additional blood work and magnetic resonance imaging. It will be at least 2 hours before the patient is ready. This is the only pelvic instrumentation available. What is the best practice in this situation?
options: Dismantle the set-up and return instrumentation to processing for resterilization.
Put tape on closed operating room doors with date, time and initials.
Cover the set-up with a sterile drape until the patient is ready.
Dismantle the set-up, flash the instrumentation and order new medical-surgical supplies.
questions.explanation: The recorded key expects dismantling the setup and returning the instruments for reprocessing after the anticipated delay. The review's older explanation rejects covering as assurance of sterility. Your 17th-edition guideline allows covering in defined circumstances with continuous monitoring; see the current-guideline note below.
optionExplanations: Matches the recorded review's intended answer for the delayed setup.
Closed doors and tape cannot establish or preserve sterility without continuous observation.
The older review rejects this option. ORNAC 17th edition permits proper covering of an intact field in specified circumstances with continuous monitoring and local policy.
IUSS is not a scheduling workaround, routine reprocessing method, or a method for sterilizing an entire set or implants.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.currentGuidance: ORNAC 17th edition §§2.17.8–2.17.11 (PDF pp. 116–117) permits proper covering of an intact sterile setup for specified circumstances, including an unexpected delay, while continuous monitoring continues. Covering never substitutes for observation. If sterility or monitoring cannot be assured, dismantle and reprocess affected supplies. The recorded key reflects the older review, not an unconditional current rule for all delays.

questions.prompt: Julia, 8 years old, fell fracturing her right radius and ulna. She ate 4 hours ago, has a penicillin allergy and two loose teeth. Julia has never had surgery but her father reports that he “had a really hard time waking up after anesthesia.” The circulating nurse is assisting with induction of general anesthesia. What presents the greatest risk for Julia?
options: Laryngospasm
Anaphylaxis
Difficult reversal
Aspiration
questions.explanation: Recent food intake and loose teeth both create aspiration concerns during induction. Clarify exactly what was eaten, assess the airway and dental risk, and plan accordingly. The family anesthetic history also needs review, but does not establish a specific inherited condition.
optionExplanations: Possible during induction, but the recent intake and loose teeth point more directly to aspiration.
The antibiotic allergy does not itself establish an anesthetic anaphylaxis event.
A vague family account does not establish a particular reversal disorder.
Best integrates the immediate food and dental airway risks in the provided scenario.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mr. Beaudoin, 34 years old, is about to undergo a right knee arthroscopy under local anesthesia. Upon exposing the knee, the circulating nurse notices several reddened and raised areas on the upper aspect of the right tibia. Mr. Beaudoin says he applied a depilatory cream the previous evening. What is the most appropriate action for the circulating nurse to take?
options: Apply waterproof spray over the reddened and raised areas before prepping.
Continue with the prep and document the rash.
Ensure skin prep is not alcohol-based.
Report the rash to the surgeon.
questions.explanation: Report the new skin reaction before preparing the operative region so the surgeon and team can assess the injury and infection risk and decide how to proceed.
optionExplanations: An aerosol does not evaluate the reaction and may add irritation or fire risk.
Proceeding without assessment leaves the new finding unresolved.
Changing solution alone does not assess the injury or determine whether surgery should proceed.
Obtains assessment of the operative-site skin abnormality before proceeding.

origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mr. Jackson, a healthy 39-year-old patient, is scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. What is a fire prevention strategy when using an alcohol-based skin prep?
options: Place absorbent pads at the periphery of the area to be prepped and remove after prepping.
Ensure that all used prep sponges are placed in a biohazardous container.
Review the chemical properties of the prep solution to determine its flammability.
Before prepping, place a dry sponge in the umbilicus to prevent pooling.
questions.explanation: Catch drips and remove the absorbent material after prep, allow the product to dry fully, and verify that solution has not pooled beneath the patient or in skin recesses.
optionExplanations: Directly prevents and removes pooled flammable solution.
Waste disposal does not directly prevent pooling or ensure drying; dispose of used material according to contamination and local policy.
Knowledge of flammability is necessary but does not physically control pooling.
A retained dry sponge can become saturated and does not provide the complete pooling-control strategy.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mr. Thompson, 56 years old with HIV, is scheduled for a lung biopsy. Which of the following infection prevention strategies should be implemented by the perioperative nurse?
options: Airborne precautions
Contact precautions
Droplet precautions
Routine practices
questions.explanation: HIV alone does not require airborne, droplet, or contact precautions. Apply routine practices and the task-specific exposure assessment; add precautions only for another suspected or known transmissible condition.
optionExplanations: HIV is not transmitted through an airborne route.
Not required solely because of HIV status.
HIV is not transmitted through ordinary respiratory droplets.
Applies the standard prevention approach without unnecessary isolation based on HIV status.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mrs. Ling, 40 years old, is scheduled for a bowel resection as the last procedure of the day in the operating room. It is noted in her health record that she is colonized with a multi-resistant organism on her skin. Which of the following actions would be the most appropriate for the perioperative nurse to take?
options: Notify cleaning staff that 10% bleach is required to terminally clean the room.
Remove all unnecessary equipment and supplies from the operating room, and don gown and gloves before direct contact with patient.
Remove all unnecessary equipment and supplies from the operating room, and put on gloves before direct contact with the patient.
Cancel and reschedule for another day.
questions.explanation: Use the indicated contact precautions and routine practices, reduce unnecessary exposed supplies, and use gown and gloves for relevant contact. Select cleaning products and concentration through the organism-specific policy and manufacturer instructions.
optionExplanations: A blanket '10% bleach' instruction is not justified for every resistant organism.
Provides the indicated barriers and reduces unnecessary exposed supplies.
Omits the gown required for the described contact-precaution approach.
Colonization alone does not automatically require cancellation.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: While setting up the back table, the perioperative scrub nurse observes that the double basin set does not have an internal chemical integrator. What would be the best practice to ensure that aseptic technique is followed?
options: Remove the double basin and ask the circulating nurse for a new double basin set.
Inform the circulating nurse that she will need a new double basin set, and remove gloves and anything else that may have come in contact with the double basin.
Continue setting up the back table since the external indicator tape changed colour and therefore there is no concern.
Ask the circulating nurse to contact the Central Supplies Department to ensure that the double basin set being used went through the sterilization cycle and that the parameters were met.
questions.explanation: Do not use a set without the required internal indicator. Replace it and assess gloves and any field items that contacted it according to the contamination procedure. An external color change alone cannot establish acceptable internal processing.
optionExplanations: Replacing the set is necessary, but this option omits assessment of contacted gloves and field items.
Addresses the unacceptable set and possible spread to the field.
External process tape does not confirm the required internal conditions.
Sterilizer records alone do not replace the missing package-level indicator.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: What are the three steps for reprocessing surgical instruments?
options: Decontaminating, handling and monitoring
Decontaminating, inspecting and sterilizing
Decontaminating, handling and sterilizing
Decontaminating, cleaning and handling
questions.explanation: The best listed summary is decontamination, inspection, and sterilization. Decontamination includes effective cleaning; preparation, packaging, monitoring, storage, and validated instructions remain part of the complete reprocessing system.
optionExplanations: Omits inspection and terminal processing.
Includes cleaning/decontamination, inspection, and sterilization in the correct broad sequence.
Omits the inspection stage.
Ends before sterilization and does not describe complete processing of critical instruments.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Why is a biological indicator used in a steam sterilizer?
options: To ensure that processed items are sterile
To ensure that all implants will be sterile following processing
To ensure that all air has been removed from the autoclave before sterilization
To ensure that the sterilizer has met the parameters necessary for sterilization
questions.explanation: A BI challenges the process with resistant microorganisms and provides evidence of its microbial lethality. It is part of sterility assurance with physical and chemical monitoring, not an absolute guarantee that every item is sterile.
optionExplanations: Overstates what a single BI result can prove about every item.
Overstates assurance for every implant and ignores the full release process.
Air-removal performance is assessed separately with the appropriate test, such as a Bowie-Dick test in applicable sterilizers; it is not what a BI measures.
Is the closest listed purpose: checking the efficacy of the sterilization process, rather than guaranteeing each item's sterility.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: In an emergency situation, what process protects the sterility of an instrument during transfer from the flash sterilizer to the sterile field?
options: Place instrument in a closed container.
Wrap instrument appropriately before flashing.
Wrap container appropriately before flashing.
Place instrument in an open pan with sterilization indicator.
questions.explanation: Use a validated closed rigid IUSS container and the approved aseptic transfer method. An arbitrary closed box is not equivalent to a container validated for the cycle and protection during transfer.
optionExplanations: Matches the protected-transfer principle when the container is validated for IUSS.
Wrapping changes the validated cycle configuration and is not an improvised substitute.
An improvised wrap is not a validated closed transfer system.
An open pan leaves the processed instrument exposed during transport.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mrs. Redshaw, 46 years old, has just undergone a dilation and curettage. After she is transferred from the operating room, the perioperative nurses observe that they did not perform a sponge count. The garbage bags have been removed from the room. What would be the most appropriate action?
options: Notify the surgeon and complete an incident report.
Agree that the sponges looked like they were are all accounted for.
Retrieve the garbage bag that is likely to be the one removed and count the sponges.
Record the count as correct because the surgeon is not prone to error.
questions.explanation: Promptly notify the surgeon that the count was omitted and initiate the missing-count and retained-item assessment protocol, with clinical documentation and a separate safety report. Imaging or further examination is decided through that protocol.
optionExplanations: Starts the necessary escalation; the complete response also assesses the patient for a retained item.
An impression cannot replace a verified count.
An unidentified garbage bag cannot reconstruct a reliable patient-specific count.
Surgeon reputation cannot establish that no item was retained.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mr. Mafett, 62 years old, is undergoing a bowel resection for an acute obstruction. There is profuse bleeding from the mesenteric artery. The circulating nurse is extremely busy obtaining additional supplies for the surgical and anesthesia providers. The scrub nurse is having difficulty obtaining and counting sponges for the surgical field. What is the best way for these nurses to deal with this situation?
options: Request additional nursing staff to help deal with the immediate situation.
Obtain additional sponges for the set-up and count the sponges only as they are used or as time permits.
Request additional medical staff to help with the immediate situation.
Inform the surgeon of the situation and conduct actions accordingly.
questions.explanation: Mobilize additional nursing help so resuscitation support, supplies, and count responsibilities can be coordinated during hemorrhage. Emergency exceptions must be communicated and documented, with reconciliation as soon as possible.
optionExplanations: Adds personnel to cover the simultaneous clinical and counting demands.
Delays verification and risks losing track of newly introduced sponges.
Additional medical help may support treatment but does not directly cover the missing nursing functions.
Communication is essential, but does not itself provide the personnel needed for simultaneous tasks.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Mr. Potter, 20 years old, is on his way to the operating room from the Emergency Department with a gunshot wound to his chest. The Emergency Department report indicates the following: T 35 °C, HR 90, RR 16 and BP 118/70. Which of the following items are most appropriate in preparing the operating room for Mr. Potter's arrival?
options: Blood warmer, warm air thermoregulatory device and warm IV solutions
Antiembolism stockings, temperature probe and disposable drapes
Warm water, adequate supply of pressure dressings and heating lamp
Positioning aids, electrosurgical unit and cardiac arrest cart
questions.explanation: A temperature of 35 °C warrants active hypothermia management. Prepare approved warming devices, warmed IV fluids, and blood warming when transfusion is indicated, while the team treats the chest injury.
optionExplanations: Provides the targeted warming resources.
Does not directly correct the identified hypothermia.
Uncontrolled heating methods risk injury and do not provide the validated warming plan.
Important general equipment, but omits targeted temperature management.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: What is the best illustration of a perioperative nurse exemplifying cost consciousness?
options: A resource nurse who coordinates the custom packs to contain standardized items
A materials coordinator who purchases surgical items based on the lowest price
A circulating nurse who opens all sterile disposable items before the start of surgery
A scrub nurse who utilizes a suture towel instead of a disposable suture book
questions.explanation: Standardized, appropriately designed packs can reduce unnecessary items, variation, and waste while preserving clinical requirements. Lowest price alone is not a sound procurement criterion.
optionExplanations: Combines standardization with reduction of unnecessary resource use.
Ignores quality, compatibility, reprocessing, and total life-cycle cost.
Creates waste when items are not needed.
A towel is not automatically an approved safe sharps-management substitute.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: The perioperative nurse observes a blistered area over the elbow of Mrs. Clarke as she is being transferred postoperatively. This was not observed preoperatively. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete an incident report and document the observation on the operating room record.
Ignore the observation because this is a common occurrence.
Document the observation on the operating room record.
Complete and document the incident report on the operating room record.
questions.explanation: Assess and treat the new skin injury, document the clinical findings, communicate them at handoff, and file the separate safety report. Do not put the incident report itself into the patient record.
optionExplanations: Provides both clinical documentation and organizational safety reporting.
A new injury requires assessment rather than dismissal.
Clinical documentation alone omits the safety-reporting process.
Document clinical observations in the record, not the incident report itself.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: Ms. Vlasek, 83 years old, is scheduled for a total hip arthroplasty. The perioperative nurse informs the surgeon that the stem size most likely required is not available in the hospital. The nurse has been informed that the implant should arrive at the hospital in about 2½ hours. What is the nurse’s best course of action?
options: Proceed with the case because the implant will be available in time for use.
Start the case when it is confirmed that the implant has arrived at the hospital.
Confirm with the surgeon that an implant has been sent and then start the case.
Confirm with the supplier that the implant is on its way and then proceed with the case.
questions.explanation: Do not begin on the assumption that a required implant will arrive in time. Confirm actual receipt, correct size, sterility or completed processing, and readiness with the team before proceeding.
optionExplanations: Estimated delivery time is not verified implant readiness.
Is the safest listed choice, with readiness and processing checks in addition to arrival.
Dispatch does not establish arrival or readiness.
A supplier's assurance that it is en route does not establish availability for use.

cases.CASE01: An adult is scheduled for a left knee procedure. During preparation, the team checks the record, consent, site mark, and planned time-out.
cases.CASE02: An adult is preparing for major abdominal surgery. The team reviews allergies, infection prevention, temperature management, and clot risk.
cases.CASE03: An anesthetized patient is transferred and positioned for a prolonged prone procedure. Skin, pressure, nerve, and handoff risks are considered.
cases.CASE04: During an open abdominal procedure, sponges are used and the closing count does not reconcile. The team must prevent an unintentionally retained item.
cases.CASE05: During surgery, a verbal order is given and specimens are sent for time-sensitive analysis. Several clear solutions are on the field.
cases.CASE06: Before anesthesia, a family history raises concern for malignant hyperthermia. The team reviews preparedness and recognition of a possible crisis.
cases.CASE07: A robotic minimally invasive operation is planned with some staff new to the platform. The team reviews docking, emergency access, and plume controls.
cases.CASE08: An urgent operation is needed for a patient with suspected respiratory infection. Airway management and subsequent room turnover require planning.
cases.CASE09: A joint replacement is scheduled. A loaned tray and implant arrive, and the team assesses validated processing and load release before use.
cases.CASE10: A head and neck procedure uses oxygen and surgical energy after skin preparation. The team is concerned about fire prevention and safe electrode handling.
cases.CASE11: An extremity operation requires a pneumatic tourniquet. The patient has fragile skin, and equipment function and inflation time need attention.
cases.CASE12: A severely injured patient is treated in the OR, with possible medicolegal evidence. The team plans preservation and, if death occurs, appropriate handling.
cases.CASE13: A pandemic surge affects an urgent surgical service. Patient routing, personnel communication, and protective-equipment supply are under review.
cases.CASE14: An OR is reviewing equipment reliability after a recall and an intraoperative malfunction. Maintenance and a safe replacement are discussed.
cases.CASE15: A reprocessing team sorts different patient-care devices by Spaulding infection-risk class and prepares them for the appropriate validated process.
cases.REC-CASE-1: Donna, the circulating nurse, is admitting 16-year-old Nina to the operating room to have a laparoscopic appendectomy. Nina is allergic to shellfish, dust and recently reacted to penicillin.
cases.REC-CASE-2: Mrs. Snider, a 44-year-old perioperative nurse, is being admitted to her own facility for a segmental resection of her left breast. Since her breast biopsy 2 weeks ago, she has thoroughly discussed the options with her surgeon and is comfortable with their joint decision.
cases.REC-CASE-3: Mr. Samson, 67 years old, is having a resection of his transverse colon with colostomy. The perioperative nurses are completing the final count. The surgeon unscrubs and sprays the incision area with a waterproof aerosol dressing which also lands on the resident's gloves. The resident activates the electrosurgical pencil to cauterize a small bleeding vessel. Flames leap along the incision and across the resident's gloves.
cases.REC-CASE-4: Chad, 16 years old, is brought to the operating room suite for open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a fractured right femur and ORIF of his left arm sustained in a motor vehicle collision. Chad received pain medication in the Emergency Department just prior to transfer to the operating room. His parents have accompanied him to the operating room, and his mother states that Chad has an allergy to penicillin. Chad does not remember when he last had something to eat or drink.
cases.REC-CASE-5: At 18:00, Dr. Jamieson calls the operating room staff to inform them that Mr. Roberts, 64 years old, will be coming to the operating room within half an hour. He has suspected intra-abdominal injuries, facial trauma and a fractured femur.

foundation.title: Professional foundations
foundation.text: Perioperative nursing integrates patient advocacy, clinical judgment, collaboration, and accountability across preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative care. A nurse practises within their role and demonstrated competence. In guideline language, shall is required, should is recommended, and may describes an option.

roles.title: Roles and competence
roles.text: Managers coordinate safe systems and resources; educators plan and evaluate learning; advanced and enhanced practice roles have defined preparation and authorization. A course or years of service alone do not prove independent competence.

routine.title: Routine and additional precautions
routine.text: Routine practices apply to every patient. A point-of-care risk assessment considers likely contact with blood, body fluids, mucosa, nonintact skin, or respiratory hazards. Additional precautions are added for a suspected or known transmission risk.

traffic.title: Traffic and respiratory controls
traffic.text: The surgical environment is managed through patient routing, room controls, limited traffic, and appropriate PPE. Airborne hazards may require a fitted respirator and a planned airway procedure; doors and clean-to-dirty flow help maintain the controlled environment.

attire.title: Attire and barriers
attire.text: Surgical attire, eye protection, masks or respirators, gowns, gloves, and surgical hand antisepsis each address different exposure pathways. Select the right barrier for the task and keep sterile gown and glove boundaries intact.

field.title: Aseptic technique
field.text: A sterile field is established close to use, observed continuously, and protected from contact, moisture, and movement outside its defined boundaries. Check package integrity before opening; treat a suspected breach as a safety concern.

prep.title: Skin preparation and draping
prep.text: Antiseptic choice and technique account for the patient, site, and product directions. Alcohol-containing products must dry and must not pool near an ignition source. Drapes create a fluid-resistant barrier but do not make an already contaminated area sterile.

devices.title: Device reprocessing
devices.text: Cleaning precedes disinfection or sterilization. Spaulding classification reflects tissue contact: critical devices enter sterile tissue and need sterilization; semicritical devices contact mucosa or nonintact skin and need at least high-level disinfection when suitable; noncritical devices contact intact skin. Follow the device-specific validated instructions.

sterile_supply.title: Sterilization and supply integrity
sterile_supply.text: Packaging, cycle monitoring, transport, storage, and traceability all affect whether a device is ready for sterile use. Immediate-use steam sterilization is for urgent unplanned needs and still requires validated processing; it is not an inventory workaround.

cleaning.title: Environmental cleaning
cleaning.text: Every case receives the scheduled environmental cleaning, with prompt management of visible contamination and additional measures when precautions require them. A clean-to-dirty workflow and approved product contact time help prevent cross-contamination.

preop.title: Preoperative verification
preop.text: Identify the patient with two approved identifiers, reconcile relevant history and allergies, verify consent and site marking, and use a meaningful team checklist. Resolve discrepancies before proceeding. Consent and advance directives require patient-centred review.

bundles.title: Perioperative prevention bundles
bundles.text: Temperature management, antimicrobial timing, wound class, VTE risk, and operative closure practices affect outcomes at different points. A bundle coordinates distinct measures while allowing patient-specific assessment and transparent documentation.

position.title: Transfer, positioning, and tissue protection
position.text: Safe transfer uses adequate personnel and aids. Positioning protects nerves, pressure areas, circulation, lines, and airway while allowing surgical access. Reassess after changes and communicate risks at handoff.

communication.title: Documentation and handoff
communication.text: Document observed care promptly and accurately. Standardized handoff conveys relevant events, unresolved issues, and required follow-up to the receiving team, with opportunity to clarify.

counts.title: Retained-item prevention
counts.text: Standardized counts track sponges, sharps, instruments, and other designated items. Personnel changes, emergency cases, intentional packing, and discrepancies require explicit communication and documentation. A correct count does not overrule a credible concern about a missing item.

specific.title: Specific care management
specific.text: Tourniquet, wound, medication, solution, and specimen handling each require checks tied to the patient and procedure. Label items clearly, reconcile time and pressure when relevant, and verify the intended specimen processing with pathology.

anesthesia.title: Anesthesia and sedation
anesthesia.text: General, regional, local, moderate sedation, and monitored anesthesia care each have different effects and preparation needs. The team plans monitoring, airway and resuscitation support, patient positioning, and safe transition to the next phase of care.

technology.title: Technology, energy, and plume
technology.text: MIS and robotic surgery require device checks and practiced emergency access. Surgical energy can cause burns or fire; coordinate oxygen, fuel, and ignition controls. Laser eyewear is hazard-specific, and surgical plume is captured near its source.

environment.title: OR environmental safety
environment.text: Lighting, noise, ventilation, temperature, humidity, electrical systems, and construction can affect patient and staff safety. Deviations are escalated through the local contingency process rather than ignored during a case.

team.title: Team and occupational safety
team.text: Credentialing, continuing education, learner supervision, and visitor controls define safe roles. Occupational risk includes biological, chemical, physical, and psychological hazards; reporting and engineering controls support safer work.

equipment.title: Equipment life cycle
equipment.text: Procurement considers clinical need, reprocessing, training, supplies, and support. Accessible instructions, preventive maintenance, recall tracking, and a malfunction response keep devices usable and traceable.

incidents.title: Incident management and disclosure
incidents.text: Near misses are intercepted before reaching a patient; no-harm incidents reach the patient without discernible harm; harmful incidents cause harm. Immediate patient care, factual documentation, reporting, review, and compassionate disclosure are coordinated through policy.

blood.title: Blood and donation
blood.text: Transfusion requires consent or documented refusal, accurate patient-product verification, monitoring, and a reaction plan. Death and donation require dignity, notification, legal considerations, and coordination with designated programs.

evidence.title: Medicolegal evidence
evidence.text: Potential evidence is identified, preserved, sealed, documented, and handed over through an approved chain of custody. Clinical care remains the priority while item identity and handling are protected.

emergency.title: Life-threatening emergencies
emergency.text: DIC, malignant hyperthermia, and cardiac arrest require early recognition, prompt communication, ready equipment, and rehearsed team roles. MH risk may be signalled by family history; rising carbon dioxide can precede fever.

pandemic.title: Pandemic response
pandemic.text: A command structure coordinates triage, patient pathways, staffing, supply, surgical priority, and education. Suspected cases are routed with precautions while status is unresolved; policies adapt as conditions change.

recording-priority.title: Selecting the best nursing action
recording-priority.text: Read the exact task: first action, anticipated equipment, risk factor, or handoff priority. Use the case findings to identify the immediate problem, then choose the action that addresses it within the nurse’s role. An option can be true in general yet less appropriate at that point. Do not invent findings that the stem does not supply.

recording-airway.title: Airway problems around anesthesia
recording-airway.text: Induction and emergence are vulnerable phases. Distinguish obstruction, difficult intubation, aspiration risk, and residual weakness. Nursing preparation includes suction, appropriate airway equipment, monitoring, and coordinated assistance. Laryngospasm is reflex glottic closure; oxygenation and airway maneuvers are urgent, with medication escalation led by the anesthesia provider.

recording-reversal.title: Neuromuscular blockade and reversal
recording-reversal.text: A neuromuscular blocker produces paralysis, not hypnosis or analgesia. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase to help reverse suitable nondepolarizing blockade; quantitative monitoring guides timing and recovery. Verify the injectable formulation and associated antimuscarinic medication. A sedative such as propofol does not reverse paralysis.

recording-last.title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity
recording-last.text: Systemic local anesthetic exposure can produce neurological symptoms, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse. Stop further exposure, summon help, and support airway and oxygenation. Activate the local LAST protocol and obtain the rescue kit, including lipid emulsion. The ASRA checklist differs from routine cardiac-arrest drug practice.

recording-allergy.title: Allergy assessment and perioperative exposures
recording-allergy.text: Identify the substance, reaction, timing, severity, and previous safe exposures. Latex sensitivity may be suggested by reactions to banana or avocado. A drug-allergy label does not identify the mechanism or automatically rule out every related drug. Communicate the history before exposure and prepare the indicated precautions and response.

recording-position.title: Individualized positioning
recording-position.text: Assess comfortable movement, joint disease, prostheses, amputations, body habitus, and skin before anesthesia. Protect ventilation, circulation, nerves, and pressure areas. In lithotomy, coordinate movement of both legs; in prone, avoid chest and abdominal compression; in lateral, protect the dependent axilla. Recheck after movement.

recording-sterile.title: A barrier breach versus a protected delay
recording-sterile.text: A torn, wet, or uncertain barrier needs assessment and immediate correction. Covering cannot sterilize contaminated supplies. An intact field during a delay is different: ORNAC permits proper covering in specified circumstances while continuous monitoring continues. If monitoring or sterility cannot be assured, replace or reprocess affected supplies.

recording-iuss.title: IUSS and sterility assurance
recording-iuss.text: IUSS is reserved for urgent, unplanned needs. Thorough cleaning, validated cycles and containers, physical checks, internal chemical indicators, daily biological testing, and traceability still apply. A chemical color change or a single negative BI is not an absolute guarantee for every item. Transfer in the validated closed container and use promptly.

recording-energy.title: Electrosurgery and the return pathway
recording-energy.text: Monopolar energy requires a suitable return electrode on clean, dry, well-perfused tissue near the operative site. Avoid scarred or compromised skin, prostheses, and unsuitable current paths. Verify the plan for implanted electronic devices. Inspect contact and skin, follow device instructions, and remove malfunctioning equipment from service.

recording-fire.title: Fire prevention and response
recording-fire.text: The fire triad consists of fuel, ignition, and an oxidizer. Prevent prep pooling, remove wet absorbent material, allow appropriate drying, and control energy devices and oxygen through team communication. During a fire, protect the patient and carry out assigned immediate control actions; safety reporting follows the emergency response.

recording-counts.title: Counts and discrepancy management
recording-counts.text: Both nurses verify countable items visually and audibly. Small incisions and few sharps do not eliminate the count or safe-containment requirements. Communicate a missing item promptly, recount and search systematically, and follow the retained-item protocol for unresolved or omitted counts. An emergency needs coordinated roles and documentation.

recording-incident.title: Injury recognition, reporting, and handoff
recording-incident.text: Assess and treat the patient first. Preserve relevant equipment and evidence, document objective clinical findings and care in the patient record, communicate follow-up needs, and complete the separate organizational safety report. Avoid attributing an unexplained injury to a patient characteristic or omitting it because it seems minor.
